items.title: Final evaluation
items.body:
## Evaluate the finished model honestly
Before shipping v0.3 you do a clean, final evaluation, one that you state as the model's real performance, using the **held-out test set you have not touched during tuning or threshold selection**. This matters because everything this week involved *choosing*: you chose hyperparameters to maximise a CV score and a threshold to fit costs, and any data used to make those choices can no longer give an unbiased performance estimate, because you optimised against it. The final test set, kept pristine, is the one honest number, so you evaluate on it once, at the end, and report that:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report, confusion_matrix
probs = best_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
preds = (probs >= chosen_threshold).astype(int)
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(y_test, probs))
print(classification_report(y_test, preds))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, preds))
```

## Report the full picture, not one flattering number
A real evaluation is several numbers read together, because each alone can mislead:
- **AUC** for threshold-independent ranking quality, your headline, comparable across versions.
- **Precision and recall at your chosen threshold**, what the model actually does in production at the cutoff you picked, the operational truth.
- **The confusion matrix**, the raw counts of true/false positives and negatives, which makes the real trade concrete: "of 1,000 late flights, we catch 780 and miss 220; of our 950 late-alerts, 780 are right and 170 are false alarms." That sentence is worth more than any single metric because it is what the model *does* to real flights.
Reporting all of these, rather than cherry-picking the best-looking one, is intellectual honesty, and it is also more useful, because the person relying on FlightWise needs to know its failure modes, not just its best statistic. A model described by one flattering number is a model whose weaknesses are hidden, from others and from you.

## Sanity-check against the baselines
Finish by comparing against the dumb baselines, because a metric only means something relative to what trivially beats it. Two baselines matter: the **majority-class baseline** (always predict "on-time"), which on imbalanced FlightWise scores high on accuracy while being useless, proving why you never trusted accuracy, and your **own earlier versions** (v0.1 logistic, v0.2 tuned-features), which show the cumulative gain from the whole foundation phase. If v0.3 clearly beats both the trivial baseline and its predecessors on the metrics that matter (AUC, recall on the late class), the work was real. If it only ties the majority baseline on accuracy, you would have learned the model is not actually predicting delay, just the base rate. Always knowing what trivially-beatable looks like is how you avoid mistaking a useless model for a working one, the single most important sanity check in applied ML.

## Where this fits
You produced FlightWise v0.3's honest final evaluation, AUC, precision/recall at your chosen threshold, and the confusion matrix, all on a pristine test set and benchmarked against trivial and prior baselines, so you can state its real performance and its failure modes plainly. The model is finished and truthfully measured. Tomorrow you tag v0.3 and ship, closing the modelling arc before the deployment week.

items.title: Tag v0.3
items.body:
## Tag v0.3 and ship the tuned model
FlightWise has reached the limit of what features and settings can give it, so you capture that as the final modelling milestone:
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "FlightWise v0.3: Optuna-tuned XGBoost + cost-based threshold"
git tag v0.3
git push origin main --tags
```
Save the tuned model and the chosen threshold together, because the threshold is part of the deployed system, not an afterthought, a model file without its operating threshold is only half the decision:
```python
import joblib
joblib.dump({"model": best_model, "threshold": chosen_threshold}, "models/flightwise_v3.pkl")
```

## Update the README with the full progression
Your version log now tells the whole foundation-phase story, and that progression is the portfolio:
```text
## Versions
- v0.1  logistic regression, raw features        test AUC 0.71
- v0.2  +5 engineered features, XGBoost           CV AUC 0.76
- v0.3  Optuna-tuned + cost-based threshold       test AUC 0.79, recall@late 0.78
```
A reviewer reading this sees a model improved deliberately across three distinct levers, features, algorithm, hyperparameters and threshold, each gain measured honestly. That narrative, *how* the model got good, is far more convincing than a single final number, because it demonstrates you understand where performance comes from and how to extract it methodically. Keep recording the validated result and the key decisions (the threshold and its cost reasoning) so the README stands on its own.

## What the foundation phase taught
Step back: in three weeks you took FlightWise from a raw-column baseline to a tuned, threshold-calibrated, honestly-evaluated classifier, and the *order* you did it in is the real lesson, features first (raise the ceiling), then algorithm (a model that can use them), then hyperparameters (extract the last gains), then threshold (fit the decision to the business), validating every step. That sequence is how strong classical ML models are actually built, and it is the opposite of flailing between algorithms hoping one works. You also built the habits that make it trustworthy: held-out evaluation, cross-validation, honest reporting against baselines. Those carry into every model you ever train, classical or deep.

## Where this fits
FlightWise v0.3 is shipped: a tuned, calibrated, well-documented model with the full v0.1-to-v0.3 improvement story in its README. You have completed the modelling arc of the foundation phase and built the core habits of honest, methodical model development. Next week you do the thing that makes a model real, take FlightWise out of the notebook and wrap it in a Flask API deployed to a public URL, so anything on the internet can ask it for a delay prediction.

weeks.title: FlightWise v0.4: Flask API
weeks.context:
A model sitting in a Jupyter notebook is not serving predictions to anyone. This week you wrap FlightWise in a Flask API, containerise it with Docker, and deploy it to a live public URL. From that point, any application, a mobile app, a browser extension, a chatbot, can call your model with a flight description and get a delay probability back.

A REST API for model serving follows a simple contract. The client sends a POST request with a JSON body containing the flight features. The server loads the model, runs predict_proba on the input, and returns a JSON response containing the delay probability and optionally the prediction confidence or feature importances. The API is stateless, every request is independent.

Flask is the right choice for a first serving deployment. It is lightweight, well-documented, and removes all the complexity of asynchronous frameworks. The limitation is throughput: Flask under default settings handles one request at a time per worker. For a portfolio project with occasional requests, this is fine. Production deployments use multiple workers (gunicorn) or switch to FastAPI for async support.

Docker is what makes your deployment reproducible. Without Docker, your model works on your laptop because of the specific versions of Python, sklearn, and XGBoost installed in your environment. On a different machine, a cloud server, a colleague's laptop, a CI container, the dependencies may differ and the model may not load. Docker packages your application and its exact dependencies into a container image that runs identically everywhere.

Deploying to Render is straightforward: push the Docker image (or connect the GitHub repo) and Render handles the rest. The deployment gives you a public HTTPS URL. For the first time in this roadmap, your model is accessible to anyone with an internet connection.

items.title: What is a REST API?
items.body:
## A model nobody can call is not a product
FlightWise v0.3 is a good model trapped in a Jupyter notebook, which means it serves predictions to exactly one person (you) on one machine. This week you free it: you wrap FlightWise in a **Flask API**, containerise it with **Docker**, and deploy it to a **live public URL**. After that, anything, a mobile app, a browser extension, a chatbot, another service, can send a flight description over HTTP and get a delay probability back. This is the step that turns a model into a product, and it is the boundary between "I trained a model" and "I shipped one that other software can use," which is most of what an ML *engineer* (as opposed to a data scientist) is hired to do.

## What an API actually is here
An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is just a contract for how other software talks to your code over the network, and a model-serving API follows a simple, stateless version of it: a client sends a request containing a flight's features, your server runs the model, and it sends back the prediction. The shape FlightWise uses is REST over HTTP:
```text
CLIENT                                  SERVER (your Flask app)
POST /predict                           load model once
{ "dep_hour": 18, "carrier": "UA",  --> run predict_proba on the input
  "origin": "ORD", "long_haul": 1 }   <-- { "delay_probability": 0.42, "late": true }
```
The key property is **stateless**: every request is independent and carries everything the server needs, the server holds no memory of previous calls, which is what lets it scale and stay simple. You are building a function that other programs can call across the internet.

## Why Flask, and what it can't do
**Flask** is the right tool for a first serving deployment precisely because it is minimal: lightweight, exhaustively documented, and free of the complexity of async frameworks, so you can stand up a working `/predict` endpoint in a few lines and focus on the serving concepts rather than fighting the framework. Its honest limitation is throughput: by default Flask handles **one request at a time per worker**, which is perfectly fine for a portfolio project with occasional traffic, and not fine for high production load. The production answer (multiple workers via gunicorn, or an async framework) is something you will note this week and grow into later; for now, Flask's simplicity is exactly what you want, because the goal is to learn deployment cleanly, not to scale to millions of requests on day one.

## Where this fits
This week completes the foundation phase by taking FlightWise from notebook to deployed service: a Flask `/predict` API, validated inputs, Dockerised for reproducibility, live on a public URL, tagged v0.4. It is the capstone of "build a model and make it real," and it sets up everything in the later Model Serving phase (W17-20), where serving, monitoring, and scaling get serious. Today's foundation: a model becomes a product when other software can call it, an API is the contract for that call, and Flask is the simple, right way to write your first one.

items.title: Install Flask
items.body:
## Install Flask and serve something trivial first
Before serving the model, you get the smallest possible web server running, because the fastest way to learn a serving framework is to make it respond to *anything* first, then add the model. Install Flask into your project environment and write a one-route app:
```bash
pip install flask
```
```python
# app.py
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000, debug=True)
```
Run `python app.py`, open `http://localhost:8000/health`, and you should see `{"status": "ok"}`. That is a working API. Everything else this week is adding routes and logic to this skeleton.

## Understand the three pieces you just wrote
This tiny app contains the whole Flask mental model, and naming the pieces makes the rest of the week obvious:
- **`app = Flask(__name__)`** creates the application, the object that routes incoming requests to your functions.
- **`@app.route("/health")`** is a *route*: it maps a URL path to the function below it, so a request to `/health` runs `health()`. Your model will live behind a `/predict` route the same way.
- **The returned dict** becomes a JSON response automatically, Flask serialises it, which is exactly the format APIs speak.
That is genuinely most of Flask. A web API is just a set of routes, each a URL mapped to a function that takes a request and returns a response, and once you see it that way, adding a `/predict` route that runs your model is a small, clear step rather than a mysterious one.

## Why a /health route earns its place
The `/health` route is not filler, it is a real production pattern you are building in from the start. A health-check endpoint lets anything, you, a deploy platform, a monitor, ask "is this service alive?" with a simple request, and platforms like Render and Fly.io (where you deploy on D6) use exactly this to know whether your container started correctly and to decide whether to send it traffic. Building it on day two means that when deployment gets complicated later in the week, you already have the simplest possible thing that proves the server is up, which is invaluable for debugging: if `/health` responds but `/predict` does not, you have instantly localised the problem to the model code rather than the server or the deploy. Starting with a trivial working endpoint and a health check is a habit that pays off every time you deploy anything.

## Where this fits
You have Flask installed and a running API skeleton: an app, a route, a JSON response, and a `/health` endpoint that proves the server is alive and that deploy platforms will use later. You understand a web API as a set of URL-to-function routes. Tomorrow you add the route that matters, `/predict`, loading FlightWise and turning a flight description into a delay probability.

items.title: Load the model + write /predict
items.body:
## Load the model once, predict on every request
Now you give the API its purpose. Two things have to happen: the trained model loads **once** when the server starts (not per request, loading a model is slow and you do it a single time), and the `/predict` route runs that loaded model on each incoming flight:
```python
import joblib
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
bundle = joblib.load("models/flightwise_v3.pkl")   # load ONCE at startup
model, threshold = bundle["model"], bundle["threshold"]

@app.route("/predict", methods=["POST"])
def predict():
    data = request.get_json()                      # the flight features
    X = build_features(data)                        # same prep as training!
    prob = float(model.predict_proba(X)[0, 1])
    return {"delay_probability": prob, "late": prob >= threshold}
```
Load-once-predict-many is the core serving pattern, and getting it right is the difference between an API that responds in milliseconds and one that reloads a model on every call and crawls.

## The deadliest trap: training/serving skew
There is one mistake here that ruins more deployed models than any other, and you must build the defence in now: **the features you compute at serving time must be produced exactly the same way as at training time.** In training you engineered `morning_rush`, `long_haul`, encoded the carrier, and so on, and the live `/predict` route has to apply the *identical* transformations to the incoming JSON, same thresholds, same encodings, same column order. If serving computes a feature even slightly differently (rush hours 7-9 instead of 6-9, a different category encoding), the model receives inputs unlike anything it trained on and its predictions silently degrade, while the API returns 200 OK the whole time. This is **training/serving skew**, and it is insidious precisely because nothing errors, the model just quietly gets worse. The fix is to share one feature-building function (`build_features`) between training and serving so there is *one* definition of every feature, never two that can drift apart.

## Ship the operating threshold, not just the model
Notice the route uses the `threshold` you saved alongside the model in v0.3, not a hardcoded 0.5. The decision boundary you tuned to the business is part of the deployed system, so it travels *with* the model in the same bundle and is applied at serve time. This is why W3 saved `{model, threshold}` together: a served model that ignores its calibrated threshold makes systematically wrong calls even though the model itself is fine. Returning both the raw probability *and* the thresholded decision is good API design too, it lets the caller use the probability with their own threshold if their cost trade-off differs from yours, while still giving the default decision. The endpoint serves the full decision, model plus threshold, exactly as you designed it.

## Where this fits
FlightWise now serves predictions: the model loads once at startup, `/predict` turns a flight JSON into a probability and a decision using the *same* feature pipeline as training (defeating training/serving skew) and the saved operating threshold. The model is genuinely callable. Tomorrow you harden the endpoint against the messy, malformed inputs the real internet will send it.

items.title: Input validation
items.body:
## The internet sends garbage; validate before you predict
Your `/predict` route currently trusts its input, and a public API must never do that, because callers will send requests with missing fields, wrong types, nonsense values, and empty bodies, sometimes by mistake, sometimes by probing. Without validation, a bad request reaches `model.predict_proba`, which throws an ugly stack trace, returns a 500 error, and possibly crashes the worker, a bad input becoming a server failure. **Input validation** is the layer that catches malformed requests at the door and returns a clear, polite error instead:
```python
REQUIRED = ["dep_hour", "carrier", "origin", "distance"]

@app.route("/predict", methods=["POST"])
def predict():
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    if not data:
        return {"error": "body must be JSON"}, 400
    missing = [f for f in REQUIRED if f not in data]
    if missing:
        return {"error": f"missing fields: {missing}"}, 400
    if not (0 <= data["dep_hour"] <= 23):
        return {"error": "dep_hour must be 0-23"}, 400
    # ... only now run the model
```

## Validation is also a correctness safeguard, not just politeness
Returning a clean 400 instead of a 500 is good manners, but validation does something more important for an ML API: it protects the *model's* correctness. A request with `dep_hour: 99` or a carrier code that never appeared in training would not crash the model, it would produce a confident, meaningless prediction, which is worse than an error because it looks valid. By rejecting out-of-range and unknown values up front, you ensure the model only ever predicts on inputs that resemble its training data, so every prediction it returns is one it is actually qualified to make. This connects straight back to training/serving skew: validation is where you enforce that serving inputs live in the same world as training inputs, turning "the model received something impossible and guessed" into "the API said no, here's why." Garbage rejected at the door is garbage that never becomes a garbage prediction.

## Use the right status codes and clear messages
Finish by speaking HTTP properly, because an API is a contract and the status code is how it communicates outcome:
- **400 Bad Request** for malformed or invalid input, the caller's fault, with a message saying exactly what was wrong (`missing fields: ['origin']`) so they can fix it.
- **200 OK** with the prediction when the request is valid.
- **500** only for genuine server errors you did not anticipate, which good validation makes rare.
Clear, specific error messages are not a nicety, they are what makes your API usable by anyone other than you: a caller who gets `missing fields: ['origin']` fixes their request in seconds, while one who gets a 500 and a stack trace is stuck. Designing the failure responses as carefully as the success response is a mark of an engineer who has actually operated an API, not just written one.

## Where this fits
Your `/predict` endpoint now validates every request, rejecting malformed and out-of-range inputs with clear 400 errors before they reach the model, which keeps the server stable *and* guarantees the model only predicts on inputs it is qualified for. FlightWise's API is robust enough to face the public internet. Tomorrow you package the whole thing in Docker so it runs identically everywhere, the prerequisite for deploying it.

items.title: Dockerize
items.body:
## Package it so it runs the same everywhere
Your API works on your machine, which raises the oldest problem in software: "it works on my machine" is not a deployment. **Docker** solves it by packaging your app together with its exact environment, the Python version, every library at its pinned version, your code and model, into a single **container image** that runs identically on your laptop, a colleague's machine, and the cloud server you deploy to. You describe the environment once in a `Dockerfile`, and Docker builds a reproducible image from it:
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]
```
Build and run it, and you are running the exact artifact you will deploy:
```bash
docker build -t flightwise .
docker run -p 8000:8000 flightwise
```

## The Dockerfile is a reproducible lab notebook
Read the Dockerfile as a precise, executable record of how to recreate your serving environment from scratch, which is exactly its value. `FROM python:3.11-slim` pins the base; `requirements.txt` pins every dependency; `COPY . .` brings in your code and the saved model; `CMD` states how to start the server. Anyone, including future-you, can rebuild the identical environment from this one file, with no "which Python did I use?" or "which pandas version?" guesswork. This is reproducibility as engineering, the same value the conda environment gave you locally, now portable to any machine that runs Docker. For ML specifically it matters double, because models are sensitive to library versions (a scikit-learn upgrade can change behaviour), so freezing the exact versions your model was trained and tested with is how you guarantee the deployed model behaves like the one you evaluated.

## Notice gunicorn quietly fixed the throughput problem
The `CMD` runs **gunicorn**, not Flask's built-in `app.run`, and that is deliberate: gunicorn is a production server that runs multiple workers, directly addressing the one-request-at-a-time limitation noted on D1. Flask's development server is fine for local testing but is single-threaded and explicitly not for production; gunicorn wraps your same Flask app and serves it with several worker processes, so the container can handle concurrent requests. You did not change a line of your application code, you changed how it is *run*, which is the clean separation Docker encourages: the app stays simple, the container decides how it is served and scaled. Building production-readiness into the container rather than the app is a pattern you will see throughout ML infrastructure.

## Where this fits
FlightWise is now a Docker image: a single reproducible artifact bundling the pinned environment, your code, and the model, served by gunicorn for real concurrency, that runs identically anywhere Docker does. The Dockerfile is your executable record of the serving environment. With a portable image in hand, tomorrow you deploy it to a public URL on Render or Fly.io.

items.title: Deploy to Render or Fly.io
items.body:
## Put it on the public internet
You have a portable container; today it goes live. Platforms like **Render** and **Fly.io** are built to take a repo (or a Docker image) and give it a public HTTPS URL with minimal fuss, which is exactly right for a portfolio deployment. The flow is straightforward: connect your GitHub repo, point the platform at your Dockerfile, set the port, and it builds and runs your container on a public address:
```text
1. Push FlightWise (with Dockerfile) to GitHub
2. Create a new Web Service on Render/Fly, link the repo
3. It detects the Dockerfile, builds the image, starts the container
4. You get  https://flightwise.onrender.com  (or .fly.dev)
5. Test:  curl -X POST https://.../predict -d '{...}' -H "Content-Type: application/json"
```
When that `curl` returns a delay probability from a server in the cloud, FlightWise is a real, callable product.

## The health check earns its keep now
Remember the `/health` route from D2? This is where it pays off. Deploy platforms use a health-check endpoint to decide whether your container started successfully and whether to route traffic to it, so you point the platform's health check at `/health`, and if the container comes up and `/health` returns ok, the platform marks the service live; if it does not, the platform knows the deploy failed and tells you, instead of silently serving a broken endpoint. This is also your first debugging tool when a deploy misbehaves: if `/health` responds but `/predict` 500s, the server deployed fine and the problem is in your model-loading or feature code; if `/health` itself is down, the container is not starting (often a missing dependency or a wrong start command). The cheap endpoint you built on day two is now the thing that tells you, in production, whether the lights are on.

## Expect the first deploy to fight you, and debug it methodically
Be ready for the first deploy to fail, because it almost always does, and knowing that turns a frustrating hour into a routine one. The usual culprits are specific and findable: the **model file is missing** (it got `.gitignore`d like the raw data, but unlike data, the model *must* ship, so commit it or fetch it at startup), a **dependency** is absent from `requirements.txt` (it worked locally because it was in your environment but not declared), the **port** the platform expects differs from the one your app binds, or **memory limits** on a free tier are too small for the model. The method is the same every time: read the platform's build and runtime logs, they tell you exactly which step failed, fix that one thing, redeploy. Methodical log-reading, rather than random changes, is the deployment skill, and the first time you debug a failed deploy from its logs is the first time deployment stops feeling like magic.

## Where this fits
FlightWise is deployed to a public URL on Render or Fly.io, with the platform's health check wired to your `/health` route and the first round of deploy failures debugged from the logs. Anyone, any program, anywhere can now ask FlightWise for a delay prediction over HTTPS. Tomorrow you tag v0.4 and write up the now-deployed system, closing the foundation phase.

items.title: Tag v0.4
items.body:
## Tag v0.4: FlightWise is live
The model is now a deployed product, the biggest milestone since v0.1, so you tag it and capture the deployed state:
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "FlightWise v0.4: Flask API, Dockerized, deployed to public URL"
git tag v0.4
git push origin main --tags
```
Update the README to reflect that FlightWise is no longer just a model but a *service*: the live URL, an example request and response, and how to run it locally with Docker. The README is now documentation a stranger could use to actually call your API, which is exactly what makes a deployed project credible.

## Document the API as a contract
A deployed API needs its contract written down, because callers need to know how to use it without reading your code:
```text
## API
POST /predict
  body:    {"dep_hour": 18, "carrier": "UA", "origin": "ORD", "distance": 1700}
  returns: {"delay_probability": 0.42, "late": true}
  errors:  400 if fields missing or out of range

GET /health -> {"status": "ok"}
```
Stating the inputs, the output, and the error behaviour turns your endpoint into something other developers (and future-you) can build against confidently. This is the same finding-plus-evidence clarity as a good analyst's memo, applied to an API: say exactly what it does and how to call it, so a reader knows without experimenting. A documented contract is the difference between an API people can use and one only you understand.

## What the whole foundation phase delivered
Four weeks, and FlightWise went the entire distance from idea to deployed product: real data cleaned into a defined target (W1), features that encode domain knowledge (W2), a tuned and threshold-calibrated model evaluated honestly (W3), and a validated, Dockerised, publicly deployed API (W4). That arc, data to model to service, with version tags marking every step, is the complete shape of an ML engineering project, and you have now done it end to end once. The deeper takeaway is that an ML engineer's job does not end at a good model; it ends at a *served* model that other software can rely on, and the deployment, validation, and reproducibility skills of this week are as central to the role as the modelling of the weeks before. FlightWise v0.1-to-v0.4 is your proof that you can carry a model all the way.

## Where this fits
FlightWise v0.4 is shipped and live: a deployed, documented, Dockerised delay-prediction API with the full foundation-phase story in its version history. You have completed the build-a-model-and-make-it-real arc. Next, the Classical ML phase (W5-8) goes deep on the algorithms you have been *using*, regression, trees and ensembles, clustering, time series, so you understand not just how to apply them but how and why they work, the foundation for choosing the right model for any problem.

weeks.title: Linear and Logistic Regression, Truly Understanding the Workhorse
weeks.context:
Logistic regression and XGBoost are powerful, but using them correctly requires understanding the mathematical principles behind them. This week you step back from FlightWise and build a loan default predictor using the Home Credit dataset, with a focus on interpretability. The goal is to produce a model where you can explain every coefficient, every decision boundary, and every prediction in terms a loan officer would understand.

Ordinary least squares regression minimises the sum of squared residuals. The closed-form solution, the normal equation, gives you the exact optimal coefficients in one matrix operation. Gradient descent arrives at the same place iteratively, which is the only option when the dataset is too large to invert the covariance matrix directly. Understanding both forms gives you intuition about when each is appropriate and what "optimal" actually means.

Logistic regression is OLS adapted for binary classification. The sigmoid function squeezes the linear combination of features into the range (0, 1), giving you a probability. The coefficients are no longer interpretable as direct effects on the outcome, they are log-odds. A coefficient of 0.5 on annual income means that a one-unit increase in income multiplies the odds of default by e^0.5 ≈ 1.65. Converting log-odds to odds ratios and then to plain language is the interpretability skill this week develops.

Regularisation prevents overfitting by penalising large coefficients. L1 (Lasso) penalty drives small coefficients to exactly zero, effectively performing feature selection. L2 (Ridge) penalty shrinks all coefficients toward zero but keeps them all non-zero. Elastic Net is a linear combination of both. For the loan predictor, where you need to explain which features matter, L1 is attractive because it produces a sparse, interpretable model. The regularisation strength (the alpha parameter) controls the tradeoff between fit and simplicity.

The interpretability requirement drives every modelling decision this week: coefficient interpretation, regularisation choice, feature scaling (you must scale features before logistic regression for coefficients to be comparable), and the final report format that presents the model to a non-technical audience.

concept_check.q: Your logistic regression model has a coefficient of -2.3 on the DAYS_EMPLOYED feature (the number of days the applicant has been employed). What does this mean in practical terms? First, check the sig?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You compare L1 and L2 regularisation on your loan predictor. L1 produces a model with 12 non-zero coefficients out of 20 features. L2 produces a model with all 20 non-zero coefficients. How do you cho?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Your model receives a feature called DAYS_BIRTH (days since birth, negative for past dates, e.g., -12000 means 12000 days old = roughly 33 years). Before training, how do you handle this? Convert it t?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: The line that fits, and why
items.body:
## Understand the workhorse, do not just call it
You have used logistic regression and XGBoost; this week you step back from FlightWise and *understand* the linear models underneath, because using a model correctly requires knowing the principles it runs on. The project is a **loan default predictor** on the Home Credit dataset, and the deliberate focus is **interpretability**: the goal is a model where you can explain every coefficient, every decision boundary, and every prediction in terms a loan officer would accept. That focus is not a limitation, it is the point, because in lending (like medicine, hiring, credit) a model you cannot explain is a model you cannot legally or ethically deploy, and linear models are the workhorse precisely because they are powerful *and* explainable.

## Why linear models still matter in a world of XGBoost
It is fair to ask why you would study linear regression when boosted trees usually score higher. Three reasons make this week essential. First, **interpretability**: a linear model's prediction is a transparent sum of "this feature contributed this much," which a loan officer, a regulator, or a doctor can audit, where a tree ensemble is a black box. Second, **foundation**: logistic regression is the conceptual seed of nearly everything later, gradient descent, the sigmoid, regularisation, even a single neuron in a neural network is logistic regression, so understanding it deeply makes deep learning far less mysterious. Third, **baseline discipline**: a well-built linear model is the honest baseline every fancier model must beat, and surprisingly often it is good enough, so reaching for XGBoost before you have a linear baseline is skipping the cheapest, clearest model that might already solve the problem.

## What "truly understanding" means this week
The week's promise is that you will not just *run* these models but grasp what they compute and why. You will see what "the best-fitting line" actually means (minimising squared error), learn the two ways to find it (the closed-form normal equation and iterative gradient descent) and when each applies, understand how logistic regression adapts the line to classification via the sigmoid, and read its coefficients as **odds ratios** a loan officer would understand. You will even build it from scratch and match scikit-learn, the surest proof you understand a model is that you can rebuild it. And you will learn **regularisation** (Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet) as the principled defence against overfitting. By Sunday, linear models will be transparent to you, not magic you invoke.

## Where this fits
This opens the Classical ML phase, where you go deep on the algorithms you have been applying. It starts with linear models because they are the most interpretable and the conceptual foundation for everything after, trees next week, then the unsupervised and time-series methods, and eventually deep learning, which is linear models stacked and bent. Today's orientation: linear models are worth deep study for their interpretability, their role as the foundation of ML, and their place as the baseline you must beat, and this week you build a loan predictor you can fully explain.

items.title: OLS and reading residuals
items.body:
## What "the best-fitting line" actually means
Linear regression fits a line (or hyperplane) through your data, but "best fit" needs a precise definition, and that definition is the heart of the method. **Ordinary least squares (OLS)** defines the best line as the one that **minimises the sum of squared residuals**, where a residual is the gap between a real data point and what the line predicts for it. You square the residuals (so positive and negative errors do not cancel, and large errors are penalised more than small ones) and sum them; the line that makes that sum smallest is the OLS solution.
```text
residual_i = y_i - prediction_i
OLS picks the coefficients that minimise  sum( residual_i^2 )
```
That is all "fitting a line" means: choosing the slope and intercept that leave the least total squared error.

## Two ways to find it, and why both matter
There are two routes to those optimal coefficients, and knowing both gives you real intuition about what "optimal" means and when each is usable:
- **The normal equation (closed form):** a single matrix operation gives you the *exact* optimal coefficients in one shot, no iteration. It is beautiful and precise, but it requires inverting a matrix whose size grows with the number of features, which becomes slow or impossible on very large or very wide datasets.
- **Gradient descent (iterative):** instead of solving exactly, you start somewhere and take repeated downhill steps on the error until you reach the same minimum. It is slower per-answer but scales to data far too large to invert directly, which is why it, not the normal equation, powers large-scale ML and all of deep learning.
The two arrive at the *same* best line on a problem where both apply; understanding that the closed form gives the exact answer when you can afford it, and gradient descent approximates it when you cannot, is the intuition this week is building (you will feel gradient descent directly tomorrow).

## Residuals are the model's confession
Once you fit OLS, **reading the residuals** is how you check whether a linear model was even the right choice, and this diagnostic habit matters more than the fit itself. You plot the residuals and look for *structure*:
```python
residuals = y_true - model.predict(X)
# plot residuals vs predictions: you want a shapeless cloud around zero
```
If the residuals are a random, patternless cloud centred on zero, the linear model captured the real structure and only noise is left, good. If the residuals show a **pattern**, a curve, a funnel that widens, clusters, the model is *systematically* wrong in a way a straight line cannot fix, which usually means the relationship is non-linear or you are missing a feature. Residuals are the model telling you where it fails, and learning to read them is what separates someone who trusts an R-squared number from someone who actually knows whether their model fits. A good score with patterned residuals is a warning, not a success.

## Where this fits
You now understand OLS precisely: the best line minimises squared residuals, you can find it exactly with the normal equation or iteratively with gradient descent (each appropriate at different scales), and reading the residuals tells you whether a linear model fits at all. This is the mathematical core of the workhorse. Tomorrow you feel gradient descent directly, the optimisation idea that powers everything from this model to GPT.

days.title: Gradient descent, felt not memorised
days.summary: Focus: Gradient descent, felt not memorised

items.title: Gradient descent, felt not memorised
items.body:
## Gradient descent, felt rather than memorised
Gradient descent is the most important optimisation idea in all of ML, and the goal today is to *feel* it, not memorise a formula, because once it clicks here it will demystify everything from this linear model to neural networks. The picture: imagine the model's error as a landscape, where each possible set of coefficients is a location and the height is how much error that model makes. Training is finding the lowest point. Gradient descent finds it the way water finds a valley, by repeatedly looking at the slope where you stand and stepping **downhill**:
```text
1. start at some coefficients (anywhere)
2. compute the gradient = the direction of steepest INCREASE in error
3. step the OPPOSITE way (downhill) by a small amount
4. repeat until the slope flattens (you're at the bottom)
```
That loop, check the slope, step downhill, repeat, is the entire algorithm, and it is genuinely simple once you see it as walking down a hill.

## The learning rate is the size of your steps
The one knob that controls gradient descent is the **learning rate**, the size of each downhill step, and understanding it intuitively explains a huge fraction of practical ML behaviour:
- **Too large** and you overshoot the valley, leaping past the bottom and bouncing around (or off to infinity), the error never settles. This is the "loss exploded to NaN" failure everyone hits.
- **Too small** and you inch downhill so slowly that training takes forever and may stall before reaching the bottom.
- **Just right** and you descend steadily to the minimum.
This is the same learning-rate knob you tuned blindly in XGBoost, now you *understand* what it does: it sets how boldly the optimiser steps toward lower error. Watching the error curve as you change it, divergence when too high, crawling when too low, smooth descent when right, builds the intuition that makes you able to debug training rather than guess.

## Why this idea is everywhere
The reason gradient descent is worth feeling deeply is that it is the universal training engine. Linear regression, logistic regression, and every neural network including the largest language models are trained by exactly this loop: define an error, compute its gradient, step downhill, repeat, just over millions or billions of parameters instead of two. The landscape is unimaginably higher-dimensional and bumpier, but the mechanism is identical to what you are watching on this loan model. So the time you spend here pays off across the entire rest of the field: when you reach deep learning and hear "we trained it with stochastic gradient descent," you will know precisely what that means, a model walking downhill on its error landscape, and concepts like learning-rate schedules, momentum, and exploding gradients will be refinements of a thing you already understand rather than new mysteries. Understand the hill once, and you understand how nearly all of modern ML learns.

## Where this fits
You now feel gradient descent: the downhill walk on an error landscape, with the learning rate setting your step size, the same engine that trains everything from this linear model to GPT. This is arguably the most transferable idea in the track. Tomorrow you apply linear modelling to the actual loan problem, classification, via logistic regression and the interpretable odds ratios a loan officer can read.

days.title: Logistic regression and odds ratios
days.summary: Focus: Logistic regression and odds ratios

items.title: Logistic regression and odds ratios
items.body:
## Logistic regression: the line, bent for yes/no
Loan default is a *classification* problem (will this loan default, yes or no?), and logistic regression is OLS adapted for exactly that. The adaptation is one piece: a linear model can output any number, but a probability must live between 0 and 1, so logistic regression takes the linear combination of features and passes it through the **sigmoid function**, an S-shaped curve that squeezes any number into the 0-to-1 range.
```text
linear part:   z = b0 + b1*income + b2*debt_ratio + ...
sigmoid:       P(default) = 1 / (1 + e^-z)      # squashes z into (0,1)
```
Everything else is the same as linear regression, you still fit coefficients by minimising an error (now via gradient descent on a classification-appropriate loss), you still get one coefficient per feature. The sigmoid is the only new idea, and it is what turns "a line" into "a probability of default."

## Reading coefficients as odds ratios
Here is where logistic regression earns its place as the interpretable workhorse: each coefficient has a concrete, explainable meaning a loan officer would accept, expressed as an **odds ratio**. A coefficient tells you how the *odds* of default change when that feature increases by one unit, and exponentiating it gives a clean multiplier:
```python
import numpy as np
odds_ratio = np.exp(model.coef_[0])   # one per feature
# e.g. debt_ratio odds ratio 1.8  ->  higher debt ratio multiplies the odds of default by 1.8
# e.g. income     odds ratio 0.6  ->  higher income multiplies the odds of default by 0.6 (protective)
```
This is the sentence a loan officer understands: "each unit of debt-to-income raises the odds of default by 80%; higher income lowers them." You can explain *every* prediction as a transparent sum of such effects, which is exactly the interpretability the project demands and exactly what a tree ensemble cannot give you. The coefficient's *sign* tells you direction (risk-increasing or protective), and its odds ratio tells you magnitude, so the model is not a black box, it is an auditable list of risk factors.

## Interpretability is a feature, not a consolation prize
The broader lesson is that logistic regression's explainability is a genuine engineering and business asset, not merely what you settle for when you cannot run XGBoost. In regulated domains, lending, insurance, healthcare, hiring, you are often *required* to explain why a model made a decision (a loan denial must come with reasons), and a model whose every prediction decomposes into named, signed risk factors satisfies that requirement natively. It also builds trust: stakeholders believe a model they can read, and they can catch its mistakes (a coefficient with a nonsensical sign reveals a data problem or leakage). So when you choose logistic regression for the loan predictor, you are making a deliberate engineering trade, accepting a possibly small accuracy cost in exchange for transparency, auditability, and trust, which in this domain is frequently the right trade, and knowing *when* explainability outweighs raw accuracy is a senior judgement the whole week is teaching.

## Where this fits
You can now build and *read* a logistic regression: the sigmoid bends the linear model into probabilities, and the coefficients translate into odds ratios that explain every prediction in a loan officer's terms, the interpretability that makes the model deployable in lending. Tomorrow you prove you truly understand it by building logistic regression from scratch and matching scikit-learn.

days.title: From scratch: match sklearn within 1%
days.summary: Focus: From scratch: match sklearn within 1%

items.title: From scratch: match sklearn within 1%
items.body:
## The proof of understanding: build it yourself
Today you build logistic regression from scratch, in NumPy, with no scikit-learn doing the work, and match sklearn's result to within 1%. This is not busywork or nostalgia; it is the surest test that you actually understand the model, because you can only rebuild what you genuinely comprehend. Everything from this week comes together in maybe thirty lines:
```python
import numpy as np
def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def fit(X, y, lr=0.1, steps=2000):
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = sigmoid(X @ w)          # predictions (sigmoid of linear part)
        grad = X.T @ (p - y) / len(y)   # gradient of the loss
        w -= lr * grad              # GRADIENT DESCENT: step downhill
    return w
```
Train this on the loan data, compare your coefficients to `sklearn.LogisticRegression`, and watch them line up. When your from-scratch model matches the library, you *know* you understand it.

## Every piece you learned this week is in those lines
Read the code and find the week in it, because that recognition is the actual learning. The **sigmoid** (D4) turns the linear part into probabilities. `X @ w` is the **linear combination** (D2), the same line-fitting from OLS. `(p - y)` is the **residual**, prediction minus truth, the model's error. The loop is **gradient descent** (D3): compute the gradient, step downhill by the learning rate, repeat, the exact downhill walk you felt earlier, now in code you wrote. Nothing in those thirty lines is new; it is everything from this week assembled. Seeing that scikit-learn's `model.fit()` is, underneath, doing precisely this loop dissolves the magic: the library is convenient and optimised, but it is not doing anything conceptually beyond what you just built, and that demystification is permanent. After this, no linear model is a black box to you.

## Why from-scratch is worth the effort once
You will not implement models by hand in your day job, you will use the libraries, so why do this? Because building it once changes how you use the libraries forever. When sklearn's logistic regression fails to converge, you know it is the gradient descent struggling (learning rate, scaling, separable data) because you have stood inside that loop. When a coefficient looks wrong, you understand it is the optimiser landing somewhere on the error landscape, not an oracle's verdict. When you reach neural networks and read "a layer is a linear transform plus a non-linearity, trained by backprop," you will recognise every word, because you built the one-layer version yourself. Implementing a model from scratch is the highest-leverage way to convert "I can call this" into "I understand this," and you only have to do it a few times in your career for the understanding to transfer everywhere. This is one of those times.

## Where this fits
You built logistic regression from scratch and matched scikit-learn, proving you understand it down to the gradient-descent loop, and you saw that the library is just a convenient wrapper around exactly what you wrote. The model is no longer magic. Tomorrow you handle the one thing the basic model still gets wrong, overfitting, with regularisation: Ridge, Lasso, and ElasticNet.

items.title: What regularisation changed
items.body: Add an L2 penalty (`+ lambda * w`) to your gradient and refit with a few lambda values. Write down what happened to the coefficient magnitudes as lambda grew. Then connect it: that shrinkage is exactly what sklearn's `C` knob controls (C = 1/lambda).

items.title: Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet, overfitting
items.body:
## When a linear model overfits, and the fix
Even a linear model can overfit, especially with many features (the loan data has plenty): it can assign large, finely-tuned coefficients that fit the training data's noise rather than the real signal, scoring well in training and poorly on new applicants. **Regularisation** is the principled defence, and the idea is elegant: add a penalty for large coefficients to the thing the model minimises, so the optimiser must balance fitting the data against keeping coefficients small. The model is no longer allowed to use huge coefficients unless they genuinely earn their keep:
```text
plain:        minimise  error
regularised:  minimise  error + (penalty on coefficient size)
```
That single addition reins in the over-confident, noise-fitting coefficients and produces a model that generalises better, the same overfitting-control theme from XGBoost's hyperparameters, now in its cleanest linear form.

## Three flavours, two behaviours
There are three standard regularisers, and the difference between them is genuinely useful:
- **Ridge (L2):** penalises the sum of *squared* coefficients. It shrinks all coefficients toward zero smoothly but rarely makes any exactly zero, so it keeps every feature, just dampened. Use it when you believe most features carry some signal and you mainly want to control overconfidence.
- **Lasso (L1):** penalises the sum of *absolute* coefficients. Crucially, it drives some coefficients **exactly to zero**, performing automatic **feature selection**, the model effectively drops the useless features. Use it when you suspect many features are irrelevant and you want a sparser, simpler model.
- **ElasticNet:** a mix of both, getting Lasso's feature-dropping plus Ridge's smooth shrinkage, useful when you have many features and some are correlated.
The key insight is that **Lasso zeros out features and Ridge does not**, which makes Lasso a tool for interpretability (a model using 12 features is easier to explain than one using 200), directly serving this week's loan-officer goal.

## The penalty strength is a bias-variance dial
Each regulariser has a strength knob (often called alpha or lambda) that controls how hard the penalty pushes, and tuning it is tuning the **bias-variance trade-off**, the central trade-off in all of supervised ML. Turn the penalty up and coefficients shrink hard: the model gets *simpler* (lower variance, less overfitting) but can become *too* simple and underfit, missing real patterns (higher bias). Turn it down toward zero and you are back to the unregularised model that may overfit. The right strength sits between, simple enough to generalise, flexible enough to capture the real signal, and you find it the honest way you already know: cross-validation, trying a range of penalty strengths and keeping the one with the best validated performance. Understanding regularisation as a bias-variance dial, not a magic "make it better" setting, is what lets you reason about *why* more penalty helps or hurts, and it is the same trade you will tune in every model for the rest of the track, made transparent here in the linear case.

## Where this fits
You can now control overfitting in linear models with regularisation: Ridge shrinks smoothly, Lasso zeros out features for a sparser interpretable model, ElasticNet blends them, and the penalty strength is the bias-variance dial you tune by cross-validation. Your loan model can now be both accurate and parsimonious. Tomorrow you assemble the fully interpretable, regularised loan default predictor and ship it.

items.title: Ship it: Loan Default Predictor
items.body:
## Ship the Loan Default Predictor
You assemble the week into a model whose every part you can explain, the deliverable the project demanded:
- a **regularised logistic regression** (likely Lasso or ElasticNet, for a sparse, explainable feature set) on the Home Credit data.
- **odds-ratio explanations** for every coefficient, so each risk factor reads in a loan officer's language.
- honest evaluation (held-out AUC, precision/recall at a cost-justified threshold) and a comparison against an unregularised baseline showing regularisation helped.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Loan default predictor: interpretable regularised logistic regression"
git push
```

## The deliverable is explanation, not just accuracy
What makes this a strong portfolio piece is not the AUC, it is that you can **explain every prediction**. Demonstrate it: take a single applicant the model flagged as high-risk and decompose the decision into its named, signed contributions, "this prediction is driven by a high debt-to-income ratio (odds ratio 1.8) and a short credit history (1.5), partly offset by high income (0.6)." That sentence is the entire point of the week, a prediction a loan officer, a regulator, or the applicant themselves could understand and challenge, which is exactly what a black-box model cannot provide and exactly what regulated lending requires. Show the global picture too (the ranked risk factors with their odds ratios) and the local picture (one applicant's explained decision), because together they prove the model is auditable, not just accurate.

## What truly understanding the workhorse gave you
Step back: this week you stopped *invoking* linear models and started *understanding* them, OLS and what "best fit" means, gradient descent as the universal training engine, the sigmoid that makes classification, coefficients as odds ratios, the from-scratch build that proved you get it, and regularisation as principled overfitting control on the bias-variance dial. That depth changes how you work everywhere: you can now reach for a linear model knowing exactly what it does and when its interpretability is worth more than a tree ensemble's accuracy, you can debug it because you understand its internals, and you have the conceptual foundation, linear combination, sigmoid, gradient descent, loss, that the rest of ML, including deep learning, is built from. Understanding the workhorse is what lets you choose it, or knowingly choose past it, rather than defaulting blindly.

## Where this fits
You shipped an interpretable, regularised loan default predictor and, more importantly, you now truly understand the linear workhorse, its math, its training, its coefficients, its regularisation, the foundation everything after builds on. Next week you go equally deep on the other tabular workhorse you have been using, trees and ensembles, understanding mechanically how decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting actually work, so you can diagnose XGBoost rather than just run it.

weeks.title: Trees and Ensembles, The Tabular Powerhouse
weeks.context:
Decision trees and ensemble methods are the workhorses of tabular machine learning. In competitions and production systems handling structured data, the kind that comes in spreadsheet rows, gradient boosted trees consistently match or outperform neural networks with less tuning and better interpretability. Understanding how they work at a mechanical level is what separates someone who runs XGBoost from someone who can diagnose when it is failing and why.

A single decision tree is interpretable but weak. It splits the training data recursively based on the feature and threshold that best separates the classes, down to a maximum depth or minimum leaf size. The splitting criterion, Gini impurity for classification, mean squared error for regression, measures how homogeneous each resulting group is. A perfect split produces groups where all members belong to one class. A useless split produces groups with the same class distribution as the parent.

Bagging (bootstrap aggregation) reduces variance. Each tree in a random forest trains on a random subset of the training data (drawn with replacement). The diversity between trees means their errors are partially uncorrelated. Averaging uncorrelated errors reduces the total error. This is the mathematical reason ensembles outperform individual trees.

Random feature subsampling, the "random" in random forest, adds another dimension of diversity. Each split considers only a random subset of features (typically sqrt(n_features) for classification). This prevents any one dominant feature from appearing in all trees, forcing the ensemble to discover diverse relationships.

Gradient boosting is different from bagging. Instead of training trees in parallel on different data subsets, it trains them sequentially. Each new tree fits the residuals (errors) of all previous trees. The ensemble improves by correcting its own mistakes. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are all gradient boosted tree implementations with different optimisations for speed, memory, and specific data types (CatBoost handles categoricals natively).

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Understand the tool you have been winning with
You used XGBoost to beat logistic regression on FlightWise, and this week you find out *why* it works, by understanding trees and ensembles at a mechanical level. On tabular data, the kind that arrives as spreadsheet rows, gradient-boosted trees consistently match or beat neural networks with less tuning and better interpretability, which is why they dominate both competitions and production systems handling structured data. The difference this week makes is the difference between someone who *runs* XGBoost and someone who can *diagnose* it: when a boosted model overfits, underperforms, or behaves strangely, understanding how the trees actually split and combine is what lets you fix it instead of randomly changing settings.

## The arc: one weak tree to a powerful ensemble
The week builds in a deliberate order that mirrors how these methods were invented, each step fixing the weakness of the last:
- **A single decision tree** is interpretable but weak, it overfits easily and is unstable.
- **Random Forest** (bagging) builds many trees on varied data and averages them, fixing the single tree's instability.
- **Gradient boosting** (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) builds trees in sequence, each correcting the last's mistakes, which is what gives the highest accuracy.
Understanding this progression, weak tree, then averaged trees, then sequentially-corrected trees, is the conceptual spine of tabular ML, and it explains why the boosted models you have been using are so strong: they are the culmination of two clever ideas (combine many trees; have each fix the previous one's errors) layered on a simple base.

## Why trees rule tabular data
It is worth knowing *why* trees, not neural nets, are the tabular default, because it shapes when you reach for each. Trees handle the messy realities of tabular data natively: they cope with mixed numeric and categorical features, do not care about feature scaling, capture non-linear relationships and feature interactions automatically (the "if evening AND hub AND winter" patterns from FlightWise), and are robust to outliers and irrelevant features. Neural networks, by contrast, want scaled, mostly-numeric inputs and large data, and they offer little interpretability on tabular problems while rarely beating a good boosted model there. So the practical rule, trees for tabular, neural nets for unstructured data like images and text, is not arbitrary; it follows from how each model works, and understanding trees this week is what lets you make that call with reasons rather than by habit.

## Where this fits
This week deepens your command of the tabular powerhouse you have been using: single trees, random forests, the boosting family (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost), their tuning, and reading them via importance and partial dependence. It pairs with last week's linear models to complete your classical-ML toolkit, the two families that handle most structured-data problems, and it builds the mechanical understanding that lets you diagnose, not just run, these models. Today's orientation: trees dominate tabular ML because of how they natively handle real data, and the path from one weak tree to a powerful ensemble is the week's spine.

items.title: Decision trees
items.body:
## How a single tree actually decides
Strip the ensemble away and understand the atom: a **decision tree** classifies by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data into ever-smaller groups. At each node it picks the *one* feature and threshold that best separates the classes, sends matching rows one way and the rest the other, and repeats on each resulting group, recursively, until it hits a stopping rule (a maximum depth, or a minimum number of rows in a leaf). To predict, you drop a new row in at the top and follow its answers down to a leaf, whose majority class (or average value) is the prediction.
```text
debt_ratio > 0.4 ?
 ├─ yes ─> credit_history < 2yr ?  ├─ yes -> DEFAULT
 │                                 └─ no  -> ok
 └─ no  ─> ok
```
That readable flowchart *is* the model, which is why a single tree is the most interpretable thing in ML.

## What "best split" means: impurity
The whole intelligence of a tree is in how it chooses each split, and it chooses the split that makes the resulting groups most **homogeneous**, measured by an impurity criterion:
- **Gini impurity** (classification): measures how mixed a group's classes are. A group that is all one class has impurity 0 (pure); a 50/50 group is maximally impure. The tree picks the split that most reduces impurity.
- **Mean squared error** (regression): the equivalent for numeric targets, picking the split that most reduces variance within the groups.
A **good split** produces groups that are each dominated by one class (high purity gain); a **useless split** produces groups with the same class mix as the parent (no gain), and the tree would not make it. So a tree is a greedy purity-maximiser: at every node it asks "which single question most cleanly separates these rows?" and takes it. Understanding impurity is understanding the tree's entire decision logic, every split is just impurity reduction.

## The single tree's fatal flaw: overfitting
A lone decision tree has a serious weakness that motivates everything else this week: left unconstrained, it keeps splitting until each leaf is pure, which means it memorises the training data, including its noise, and **overfits** badly. A deep tree can carve out a tiny leaf for every quirk in the training set, scoring perfectly there and generalising poorly to new data. It is also **unstable**: change a few training rows and the greedy splits can cascade into a completely different tree, so single trees are high-variance. You can limit a tree (cap its depth, require a minimum leaf size, which you should), but that trades away accuracy for stability, you get a weak, stable model or a strong, overfit one. This dilemma, single trees are either weak or overfit, is exactly the problem that ensembles solve, and seeing it clearly is what makes random forests and boosting feel like the natural fixes they are.

## Where this fits
You understand the decision tree: it splits greedily on the feature/threshold that most reduces impurity (Gini or MSE), reads as an interpretable flowchart, and overfits badly because it memorises noise unless constrained. That overfitting-versus-weakness dilemma is the setup for the rest of the week. Tomorrow you meet the first fix, random forests, which tame the single tree's instability by combining many of them.

items.title: Random Forest
items.body:
## Many trees beat one: the random forest
A single tree overfits and is unstable; a **random forest** fixes both by building *many* trees and averaging their predictions. The core technique is **bagging** (bootstrap aggregation): you train each tree on a different random sample of the data (drawn with replacement, so each tree sees a slightly different dataset), and to predict, you let all the trees vote and take the average (or majority). The magic is in the averaging: individual trees overfit in *different* directions because they saw different data, so their errors partly cancel, and the averaged prediction is far more stable and accurate than any single tree. You trade the single tree's readability for a big gain in reliability.
```text
data --> sample 1 --> tree 1 \
     --> sample 2 --> tree 2  >--> average the votes --> stable prediction
     --> sample N --> tree N /
```

## Why averaging works: decorrelated errors
The reason a forest beats a tree is worth understanding precisely, because it is one of the most important ideas in ML. Averaging many predictors reduces **variance** *only if their errors are not identical*, if every tree made the same mistakes, averaging would not help. So random forests work hard to make the trees *different* from each other: bagging gives each tree different rows, and a second trick, **random feature selection**, gives each split only a random subset of features to choose from, so the trees cannot all lock onto the same dominant feature. These two sources of randomness **decorrelate** the trees, making their errors independent enough that averaging cancels them out. This is the deep lesson: an ensemble's power comes from its members being individually good *and* collectively diverse, the same principle behind asking a crowd of varied experts instead of one. Understanding "diverse, decorrelated learners average to something better than any one" explains not just random forests but every ensemble method.

## Forests are strong, low-tuning, and honest about importance
Practically, random forests are a fantastic default: they are robust, hard to overfit (more trees never hurts, unlike a deeper single tree), need little tuning to work well, and give a reliable feature-importance signal as a byproduct. They have a free built-in validation trick too, **out-of-bag (OOB) error**: since each tree was trained on a bootstrap sample, the rows it did *not* see can serve as its test set, giving an honest performance estimate without a separate split. Where forests fall slightly short is peak accuracy, because they build trees *independently* (in parallel) and only average them, they cannot have later trees *learn from* earlier trees' mistakes. That limitation is exactly what boosting addresses, and it is why, although random forests are excellent and underrated, gradient boosting usually edges them out on accuracy. Knowing the trade, forests are simpler and more robust, boosting is more accurate but more delicate, lets you pick deliberately.

## Where this fits
You understand random forests: bagging plus random feature selection builds diverse, decorrelated trees whose averaged vote is stable and accurate, fixing the single tree's overfitting and instability, with OOB error as a free honest estimate. You also see the forest's one limit, its trees do not learn from each other. Tomorrow you meet the methods that do, the gradient-boosting family you have been using: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost.

days.title: XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost
days.summary: Focus: XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost

items.title: XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost
items.body:
## Boosting: trees that correct each other
Random forests build trees independently and average them; **gradient boosting** builds trees *sequentially*, each one trained to fix the errors the previous trees made. You start with a weak prediction, look at where it was wrong (the residuals), and train the next tree specifically to correct those mistakes, then add it in; repeat, and the ensemble steadily improves by focusing each new tree on what is still wrong. This "learn from the previous model's errors" loop is why boosting reaches higher accuracy than bagging: a forest's trees cannot help each other, but a boosted model's trees are a relay team, each picking up exactly where the last fell short.
```text
forest:    trees vote in parallel, errors cancel by averaging
boosting:  tree1 -> residuals -> tree2 fixes them -> residuals -> tree3 fixes those -> ...
```
This is the algorithm behind the XGBoost you have been winning with; now you know what it is doing.

## Three implementations of the same idea
XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost all implement gradient boosting; they differ in engineering trade-offs, and knowing the differences helps you pick:
- **XGBoost:** the established, battle-tested default, excellent accuracy, huge ecosystem, strong regularisation. The safe baseline, what you have been using.
- **LightGBM:** built for **speed and large datasets**. It grows trees leaf-wise (rather than level-wise) and bins features, making it dramatically faster on big data, at a slightly higher overfitting risk on small data. Reach for it when training time or data size is the constraint.
- **CatBoost:** built to handle **categorical features** natively and gracefully, with strong defaults that resist overfitting and need little tuning. Reach for it when you have many categorical columns (it spares you a lot of manual encoding) or want strong results out of the box.
They are interchangeable enough that you can try all three on a problem and keep the best, but understanding each one's strength, XGBoost reliable, LightGBM fast, CatBoost categorical-friendly, lets you choose with intent.

## Boosting's power is also its danger
The same sequential error-correction that makes boosting accurate makes it **prone to overfitting** in a way random forests are not, and this is the single most important practical fact about it. Because each tree is added to reduce the *training* error further, a boosted model will, if unchecked, keep fitting the training data, eventually memorising its noise, more trees can make it *worse* on new data, the opposite of a random forest where more trees never hurt. This is why boosting needs careful control (the learning rate, tree depth, number of trees, regularisation, early stopping) where forests largely tune themselves, and it is exactly why tomorrow's lesson on tuning boosting matters so much. The mental model to carry: a random forest is forgiving and a boosted model is powerful-but-delicate, you must hold it back from overfitting, which is the price of its higher accuracy. Knowing this turns "XGBoost is overfitting and I don't know why" into "of course, I need to slow the learning and constrain the trees."

## Where this fits
You understand gradient boosting, sequential trees each correcting the last's errors, which is why it out-accuracies random forests, and you know the three implementations (XGBoost reliable, LightGBM fast, CatBoost categorical) and boosting's defining risk: it overfits if you do not hold it back. That risk sets up tomorrow, where you learn to tune boosting's hyperparameters to get its accuracy without its overfitting.

items.title: Hyperparameter tuning for boosting
items.body:
## Tuning boosting is mostly controlling overfitting
Because boosting is powerful but prone to overfitting, tuning it is largely about *restraint*, and a handful of hyperparameters do almost all the work. Understanding what each one controls (not just sweeping them blindly, as you could in W3) lets you tune deliberately:
- **learning_rate** (eta): how much each new tree contributes. Lower means each tree corrects more cautiously, so the model learns slowly and generalises better, but needs more trees. The central accuracy-vs-overfitting knob.
- **n_estimators:** how many trees. More trees fit more, so this trades with learning rate, low learning rate plus many trees is the classic strong-and-safe combination.
- **max_depth:** how complex each tree is. Shallow trees (3-6) are weak individual learners that boost well and resist overfitting; deep trees overfit fast. Boosting wants *weak* learners, so keep depth modest.
- **subsample / colsample_bytree:** the fraction of rows/features each tree sees. Below 1.0 adds randomness (like bagging inside boosting), which fights overfitting.
- **regularisation (lambda, alpha, min_child_weight):** direct penalties on complexity.

## The learning-rate / n_estimators dance
The most important tuning relationship is between learning rate and number of trees, and seeing it clearly prevents a lot of fumbling. They trade off: a **high** learning rate with **few** trees learns fast but coarsely and overfits readily; a **low** learning rate with **many** trees learns slowly and finely and generalises best, which is why the standard recipe for a strong boosted model is "small learning rate, lots of trees, with early stopping to find the right number." **Early stopping** is the tool that makes this practical: you watch performance on a validation set as trees are added and stop when it stops improving, so you do not have to guess `n_estimators`, the model tells you when adding more trees starts hurting. This is the disciplined way to tune boosting: set a low learning rate, allow many trees, and let early stopping pick the count, rather than manually searching the two together. Combined with Optuna (W3) for the depth and regularisation knobs, you have a principled tuning workflow rather than a random sweep.

## Tune against honest validation, always
Every tuning decision here must be judged on **held-out or cross-validated** performance, never training performance, and with boosting this matters more than with any model you have met, precisely because it overfits so willingly. The defining symptom to watch is the **gap between training and validation scores**: a model with near-perfect training accuracy and mediocre validation accuracy is overfitting, and the cure is *more* restraint (lower learning rate, shallower trees, more subsampling, stronger regularisation, fewer trees via early stopping). You are tuning to *close that gap* while keeping validation performance high, which is the bias-variance trade-off from last week in action. The engineer who understands this watches the train/validation gap as the primary signal and knows that with boosting, when in doubt, slow it down and constrain it. That single diagnostic, read the gap, add restraint if it is wide, is what separates tuning boosting with understanding from poking at hyperparameters and hoping.

## Where this fits
You can now tune boosting deliberately: the key knobs are overfitting controls (learning rate, depth, subsampling, regularisation), the low-learning-rate-plus-many-trees-with-early-stopping recipe is the strong-and-safe default, and the train/validation gap is your guiding signal, always judged on honest validation. Your boosted models can now reach their accuracy without overfitting. Tomorrow you learn to read what these powerful-but-opaque models actually learned, via feature importance and partial dependence.
